lessons.title: Hydroponic systems and set-up
lessons.html:
Growing without soil

Hydroponics grows plants in a nutrient solution, with or without an inert growing medium. In South Africa it is widely used in tunnels and greenhouses for tomatoes, cucumbers, peppers, lettuce, herbs and strawberries, especially near city markets. It allows high yields per square metre and efficient water use, but needs capital, technical skill and constant management because there is little buffer if something goes wrong.

Main system types

SystemHow it worksTypical crops
Open bag or slab systemsPlants in bags of coir, sawdust or similar, fed by drippers; excess drains awayTomatoes, cucumbers, peppers
Nutrient film technique (NFT)A thin film of solution flows along gullies past the roots and is recirculatedLettuce, herbs
Deep water culture (floating rafts)Plants float on rafts over aerated solutionLettuce, leafy greens
Ebb and flowTrays flooded and drained periodicallySeedlings, potted plants

Infrastructure

  • Structure: tunnels or greenhouses with shade or plastic cover suited to the climate; insect netting for pest exclusion.
  • Water: reliable source of good quality; test for salinity, sodium, bicarbonates and microbes. Many units use filtered borehole or rainwater.
  • Fertigation: tanks for stock solutions, dosing system or injectors, filters, pumps and timers.
  • Power backup: pumps and aeration fail during load-shedding; NFT roots can dry and die quickly, so a generator, battery or solar backup is essential.
  • Climate control: ventilation, fans, pad-and-fan cooling or heating where needed.

Before investing, budget the capital cost, production cost per kg and expected market price, and secure a market.

lessons.title: Managing the nutrient solution
lessons.html:
The heart of the system

Plants depend completely on the nutrient solution for water and nutrients, so it must be managed precisely.

Formulating the solution

Use a recipe designed for the crop and stage, supplied by a hydroponic fertiliser supplier or consultant. Solutions are usually made from two concentrated stock tanks (often called A and B) so that calcium does not react with sulphates and phosphates and precipitate. Never mix the concentrates together undiluted.

Electrical conductivity (EC)

EC measures the total concentration of dissolved salts. Too low and plants are underfed; too high and they suffer salt stress or root burn. Target EC depends on crop, growth stage and climate; follow your recipe. Measure EC of the feed and of the drainage (runoff) daily.

pH

pH controls nutrient availability. Most crops do well in a slightly acidic range set by the recipe. Adjust with acid or alkali dosing, carefully.

Daily routine

  1. Check feed EC and pH; calibrate meters regularly with standard solutions.
  2. Measure drain volume and EC: drain percentage shows whether plants receive enough solution.
  3. Check drippers or gullies for blockages and even flow.
  4. Record readings, irrigation cycles and weather.
  5. Inspect plants for deficiency or toxicity symptoms.

Recirculating systems

In NFT and floating systems, nutrients get used unevenly and pathogens can spread through the solution. Top up and adjust daily, replace solution periodically and consider disinfection (UV, filtration) of recirculated water.

Safety

Acids and concentrated fertilisers can burn skin and eyes. Wear gloves, goggles and an apron, add acid to water (never water to acid), store chemicals separately and have water for eye washing nearby.

lessons.title: Crop, pest and business management
lessons.html:
Running a profitable unit

Crop management

  • Use disease-free seedlings from reputable nurseries.
  • For vine crops, train plants on strings, remove side shoots, lower and lean stems and remove old leaves regularly.
  • Pollinate tomatoes with bumblebees where permitted, vibration tools or good air movement.
  • Manage temperature and humidity: high humidity favours fungal diseases; very high temperatures cause flower drop.

Integrated pest management

Insect netting, double doors, sticky traps and weekly scouting form the base. Common pests include whitefly, thrips, red spider mite and Tuta absoluta in tomatoes; diseases include powdery mildew, botrytis and root rots such as Pythium. Use biological control agents where available and registered agrochemicals only according to the label, observing pre-harvest intervals. Disinfect between crops and keep the area around tunnels weed-free.

Hygiene and food safety

Staff must wash hands, use clean harvesting crates and keep produce off the floor. Keep spray records for buyer audits.

Business management

MeasurePurpose
Yield per m² per weekProduction efficiency
Cost per kgProfitability
Grade-out % (class 1)Quality and price
Water and fertiliser use per kgResource efficiency

Plan planting dates to supply the market continuously or to hit higher-price windows, and spread sales between fresh produce markets, retailers and local buyers.

Key points

  • Choose a system that fits the crop, market and skills available.
  • Manage EC and pH daily and record readings.
  • Keep A and B concentrates separate and handle acids safely.
  • Have backup power; root systems fail fast without water.
  • Use IPM, hygiene and cost-per-kg records to stay profitable.
